title: Rain, Dew and Weather
lead: The promised land "drinks water from the rain of the sky" (Deuteronomy 11:11). So the Bible watches the weather closely: the early and late rains, dew, wind, thunder, snow and hail. All of them are sent by God. Drought and hunger have their own page (Famine).

sections.h: A land that waits for rain
sections.b:
In Egypt a farmer "watered it with your foot, like a vegetable garden." But the promised land "is a land of hills and valleys" that depends on rain from God (Deuteronomy 11:10–12). He promises "its rain at the right time, the early rain and the late rain" (Deuteronomy 11:14). The Hebrew words are yoreh (also moreh), the autumn rain, and malqosh, the spring rain. Jeremiah speaks of God "who gives rain, the autumn and the spring rain, / each at its time" (Jeremiah 5:24; compare Joel 2:23; Hosea 6:3; Zechariah 10:1). James borrows the picture: the farmer waits "until it receives the early and the late rains" (James 5:7).

Dew mattered too, as a blessing (Genesis 27:28; Hosea 14:5) and as a sign for Gideon (Judges 6:37–40). Samuel called down thunder and rain at the wheat harvest as a sign (1 Samuel 12:17–18). After the flood God promises that "seedtime and harvest, cold and heat" will not stop (Genesis 8:22), and he sets his bow in the clouds (Genesis 9:13).

Jewish prayer still follows this year. The Mishnah records a debate over when to begin mentioning "the might of the rains." Rabbi Eliezer says from the first day of Sukkot, the autumn feast. Rabbi Yehoshua says from its last day. Prayer for rain itself begins in the month of Marheshvan and goes on until about Passover (Mishnah Taanit 1:1–3).

sections.h: Rain from the LORD, not from Baal
sections.b:
Hosea pictures Israel thanking her "lovers" for her food and oil. God answers, "She never realized that I am the one who gave her grain, new wine and fresh oil" (Hosea 2:8). Elijah's challenge is about the same question: "If the LORD is the God, go after him. If Baal is, go after him" (1 Kings 18:21). He says "these coming years will have no dew and no rain unless I give the word" (1 Kings 17:1). The drought ends with "a little cloud, like a person's hand" rising from the sea (1 Kings 18:44; compare James 5:17–18). Jeremiah asks, "Can any of the nations' empty idols make it rain?" (Jeremiah 14:22).

Thunder is "The LORD's voice" (Psalm 29:3–9; Job 37:2–5). He "lets the wind out of his storerooms" (Psalm 135:7). He asks Job, "Have you walked into the places where snow is stored?" (Job 38:22; compare Psalm 147:16–18). Hail falls on Egypt (Exodus 9:23–24) and on the armies fleeing down the slope of Beth-horon (Joshua 10:11). The hot east wind withers grain (Genesis 41:6), drives back the sea (Exodus 14:21) and strikes Jonah (Jonah 4:8). Jesus stills the wind with a word (Mark 4:39). He teaches that the Father "sends rain on righteous and unrighteous people" alike (Matthew 5:45; compare Acts 14:17).

Jesus also expects people to read the sky. A cloud from the west means rain, and a south wind means heat (Luke 12:54–55). A red sky at evening means good weather (Matthew 16:2–3; some Greek copies lack these sayings, see the note on Matthew 16:2). His complaint is that they read the weather but not the time they are living in.

sections.b:
Several verses describe water going round. "All the streams go to the sea, / and still the sea is not full" (Ecclesiastes 1:7). God "pulls up the water drop by drop; / they filter into rain from his mist" (Job 36:27). He "summons the sea's waters / and pours them out over the face of the earth" (Amos 9:6; Amos 5:8). He "lifts the clouds from the edge of the earth" (Psalm 135:7). The Greek of Job 36:27 reads differently: the drops of rain are numbered by God.

Readers explain these verses in different ways. Ray Comfort sees in them the water cycle, "something not fully understood until the 17th century, but so well brought out in the Bible." Rashi, in the Middle Ages, read Ecclesiastes 1:7 another way. The rivers' water, he said, flows back to its sources through tunnels under the mountains. In the same comment he also cites Amos 5:8, on God summoning the sea's waters and pouring them out. On every reading, the Bible's point is that the whole round of water is in God's hands.
